quote: And then I just got a, like, a Tesla.
stewart_read: Customer discloses two EVs, one purchased very recently, plus an explicit statement that consumption will keep rising over the next couple years. This is a textbook usage-growth signal that strengthens the case for solar sizing.
coaching_implication: Rep should reflect this back explicitly ('so your usage is only going up from here') to build curiosity and give the closer a strong opening data point; instead it was acknowledged with a tangent about Tesla self-parking and never revisited.

quote: is it I got one question just personal. Does it really back up itself, Tesla?
stewart_read: Rep turns a strong qualifying moment into personal small talk about Tesla's self-parking feature, unrelated to solar qualification or the appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as rapport-building small talk rather than scope creep, since it's brief and the customer enjoys it ("That's insane. That's crazy.").
coaching_implication: Light rapport banter is fine in small doses, but the manager should note this ate time and attention right after a strong usage-growth disclosure that deserved a direct follow-up instead.

quote: My my wife and I are on the title.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a co-owner on the title early in the call. The rep never circles back to confirm whether the wife will be present for the in-person appointment before booking Michael alone for 10AM.
alternative_hypothesis: The appointment is in-person at the home, so the wife may naturally be present without needing an explicit invite — but the rep never confirms this assumption on the call.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to explicitly ask 'will your wife be able to join us tomorrow at 10?' before locking the time — this is a five-second confirmation that protects the appointment from a mid-close derail if she's not home.

quote: our issue is that we have a slate roof. So it's ideally, we would want a lot of ground mount solar panels, like, in our backyard and front yard to kind of, avoid doing any kind of structural damage because it's a rock it's basically like a rock roof.
stewart_read: Customer raises a significant design constraint (slate roof, preference for ground mount) unprompted. Rep logs it with a flat 'Okay' and never asks a clarifying follow-up or builds curiosity around how the design might handle this.
alternative_hypothesis: This is closer-tier design content, so the rep may be correct to simply capture it and defer detail to the closer rather than engage further.
coaching_implication: A single follow-up like 'good to know, they'll factor that into the design' would acknowledge the concern without over-engaging; right now it's just filed and moved past.

quote: No. It won't let me in the the website because I'm I'm not I don't have an account or anything. I just if you could just screenshot, like, where the graph is, that's good enough.
stewart_read: Rep hits a technical snag trying to log into the customer's utility portal and recovers quickly by asking for a screenshot instead, staying within the 1-2 minute friction budget.
coaching_implication: This is a positive example of fast pivot on tech friction — worth pointing out to the rep as what they did right, not just what to fix.

quote: Would it be, like, an in person or just like a a a conversation?
stewart_read: Customer asks a basic logistics question about appointment format relatively late, suggesting the rep hadn't clarified in-person vs phone earlier in the call.
alternative_hypothesis: This could just be a normal clarifying question with no deeper meaning, since the customer accepts the in-person format immediately after being told.
coaching_implication: Minor, but stating up front that the appointment is a 20-30 minute in-person visit (before asking for a date) would avoid the customer needing to ask.
